notes: ELEV8MI v34 constellation/star popup text. Keys: constellations by IAU abbreviation (must exist in assets/sky/night-sky.json lines); stars by Hipparcos number (must exist in night-sky.json stars). Seasons are for Northern Hemisphere evenings (about 9 PM). Magnitudes are apparent visual magnitudes; distances in light-years (rounded, well-established values; uncertain ones are marked or omitted).

Aur.name: Auriga
Aur.myth: Often identified with Erichthonius, a legendary king of Athens said to have invented the four-horse chariot. Its brightest star, Capella, is the she-goat Amalthea, who nursed the infant Zeus.

Boo.name: Boötes
Boo.myth: Pictured as a herdsman driving the Great Bear around the pole. In some Greek versions he is Arcas, the son of Callisto.

Cnc.name: Cancer
Cnc.myth: The crab Hera sent to nip at Heracles while he fought the Hydra. He crushed it underfoot, and Hera set it among the stars.

CMa.name: Canis Major
CMa.myth: The larger of Orion's two hunting dogs, following its master across the sky. Some tellings make it Laelaps, a dog that never failed to catch what it chased.

CMi.name: Canis Minor
CMi.myth: The smaller of Orion's two hunting dogs, trotting just ahead of Canis Major.

Cas.name: Cassiopeia
Cas.myth: A vain queen of Ethiopia who boasted that she (or her daughter Andromeda) was lovelier than the sea nymphs. As punishment she circles the pole on her throne, hanging upside down for part of each night.

Cep.name: Cepheus
Cep.myth: King of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda, placed in the sky beside his queen.

Dra.name: Draco
Dra.myth: Usually Ladon, the serpent-dragon that guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides until Heracles slew it on his eleventh labor.

Gem.name: Gemini
Gem.myth: The twin brothers Castor and Pollux. When mortal Castor was killed, immortal Pollux asked to share his immortality with him, so Zeus set the pair in the sky together.

Leo.name: Leo
Leo.myth: The Nemean Lion, whose hide no weapon could pierce. Heracles strangled it as his first labor and afterwards wore its skin.

Lyn.name: Lynx
Lyn.myth: A modern constellation with no classical myth. Johannes Hevelius created it in the 1680s, reportedly saying you would need the eyes of a lynx to see its faint stars.

Ori.name: Orion
Ori.myth: A giant hunter of Greek myth. In one version he boasted he could kill every animal on Earth, and a scorpion was sent to sting him; the two were placed on opposite sides of the sky, so Orion sets as Scorpius rises.

Per.name: Perseus
Per.myth: The son of Zeus who cut off the head of the Gorgon Medusa and then rescued Andromeda from a sea monster.

Tau.name: Taurus
Tau.myth: Zeus took the form of a gentle white bull to carry the princess Europa across the sea to Crete.

UMa.name: Ursa Major
UMa.myth: The nymph Callisto, loved by Zeus and turned into a bear. Zeus later placed her in the sky, where her tail forms the handle of the Big Dipper.

UMi.name: Ursa Minor
UMi.myth: In some Greek versions it is Arcas, Callisto's son, set beside his mother; others say it honors Cynosura, a nymph who cared for the infant Zeus.
UMi.season: All year (circumpolar), highest on early summer evenings

11767.name: Polaris
11767.what: The North Star: a yellow-white supergiant and Cepheid variable at the end of the Little Dipper's handle.
11767.fact: It sits less than a degree from the north celestial pole, so it barely moves while the rest of the sky turns, and its height above your horizon roughly equals your latitude.

72607.name: Kochab
72607.what: An orange giant at the bowl of the Little Dipper.
72607.fact: Because Earth's axis slowly wobbles (precession), Kochab was the brightest star near the north pole around 1000 BC, long before Polaris took the job.

68756.name: Thuban
68756.what: A white giant in the tail of Draco.
68756.fact: About 4,700 years ago, when the Egyptian pyramids were being built, Thuban was the pole star.

54061.name: Dubhe
54061.what: An orange giant at the lip of the Big Dipper's bowl.
54061.fact: Dubhe and Merak are the Pointers: follow the line from Merak through Dubhe about five times their separation and you reach Polaris.

65378.name: Mizar
65378.what: The middle star of the Big Dipper's handle.
65378.fact: With its fainter neighbor Alcor it makes a famous naked-eye pair, long used as an eyesight test, and Mizar itself was one of the first double stars seen through a telescope.

67301.name: Alkaid
67301.what: A hot blue-white star at the tip of the Big Dipper's handle.
67301.fact: Unlike the five middle stars of the Dipper, Alkaid is not part of the group that moves through space together, so over many thousands of years the Dipper's shape will change.

24608.name: Capella
24608.what: The brightest star in Auriga, actually two yellow giant stars orbiting each other.
24608.fact: Its two giants circle each other every 104 days, far too close to split by eye; together they make the sixth-brightest star in the night sky.

15863.name: Mirfak
15863.what: A yellow-white supergiant, the brightest star in Perseus.
15863.fact: It is the brightest member of the Alpha Persei Cluster, a loose swarm of young stars that looks lovely in binoculars.

21421.name: Aldebaran
21421.what: An orange giant that marks the eye of Taurus the Bull.
21421.fact: It looks like part of the V-shaped Hyades cluster, but it is only about half as far away and just happens to lie in the same direction.

25428.name: Elnath
25428.what: A blue-white giant marking the tip of the Bull's northern horn.
25428.fact: It also completes the pentagon of Auriga, and old star charts listed it as Gamma Aurigae as well.

17702.name: Alcyone
17702.what: The brightest star of the Pleiades, the Seven Sisters cluster.
17702.fact: The Pleiades are a young cluster, roughly 100 million years old, so their hot blue stars were born after the dinosaurs were already roaming Earth.

27989.name: Betelgeuse
27989.what: A red supergiant marking Orion's shoulder.
27989.fact: It is so large that, placed where the Sun is, it would reach beyond the orbit of Mars. In 2019–2020 it faded dramatically in the 'Great Dimming', most likely hidden by a cloud of dust it had thrown off.

24436.name: Rigel
24436.what: A blue-white supergiant marking Orion's foot.
24436.fact: Despite its 'Beta' label it is usually brighter than Betelgeuse, and it gives off roughly 100,000 times more light than the Sun.

25336.name: Bellatrix
25336.what: A hot blue giant marking Orion's other shoulder.
25336.fact: Its name is Latin for 'female warrior'.

26311.name: Alnilam
26311.what: A blue supergiant, the middle star of Orion's Belt.
26311.fact: It is the most distant and most luminous of the three belt stars, even though all three look much alike.

32349.name: Sirius
32349.what: The Dog Star, the brightest star in the night sky.
32349.fact: It has a faint companion, Sirius B, a white dwarf about the size of Earth but with roughly the mass of the Sun.

33579.name: Adhara
33579.what: A blue giant in the hind leg of Canis Major.
33579.fact: About 4.7 million years ago it passed much closer to the Sun and was the brightest star in Earth's sky, outshining today's Sirius.

37279.name: Procyon
37279.what: A yellow-white star, one of our close neighbors.
37279.fact: Its name means 'before the dog' in Greek, because from northern latitudes it rises shortly before Sirius, the Dog Star.

36850.name: Castor
36850.what: One of the Gemini twins, a bright white star system.
36850.fact: A telescope splits it into two stars, and each of those, plus a faint third companion, is itself a close pair: six stars in all.

37826.name: Pollux
37826.what: An orange giant, the other Gemini twin.
37826.fact: It is the closest giant star to the Sun, and a giant planet was found orbiting it in 2006.

49669.name: Regulus
49669.what: A blue-white star marking the heart of Leo.
49669.fact: It spins so fast, about once every 16 hours, that it bulges at its equator; it also lies almost on the Sun's path, so the Moon often passes in front of it.
